But your only path to safety lies across a bridge that will hold only one person, and there is already a man on it; if you rush onto the bridge, he will be toppled off it into the valley below” (“Self-Defense,” 290).

19. For an argument on why physical obstructors should be regarded as threats, see Helen Frowe, “Threats, Bystanders and Obstructors,” *Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society* 108 (2008): 365–72.

Becoming a moral obstacle is only one of the many ways in which we can give rise to cost. In addition to giving rise to cost by being an obstacle, an obstructor, or a threat, we might give rise to cost through our agency, for instance, when we do or enable harm. The case of the moral obstacle is special, however, because the person's presence does not diminish or otherwise affect the effectiveness of the threatened person's use of defensive means. The decision about whether his presence will make the defending party worse off is entirely in the hands of the defending party. That is not always true of physical obstructors and threats; they may actually make the person under threat worse off by making it impossible for her to escape (obstructors) or simply by landing on her (threats).

Quite a few philosophers argue that mere causal contribution to harm is morally insignificant for the question of defensive force.<sup>20</sup> On this view, to be *liable* to defensive force, that is, to forfeit one's right against such harm, a person must be morally responsible for an unjust threat to others. Innocent and nonresponsible threats (as well as obstacles and obstructors) are therefore indistinguishable from innocent bystanders when it comes to liability to harm. These philosophers are, of course, not arguing against the significance of the causal contribution of moral obstacles (making people unable to avoid harm without harming others) since this is a category that they have not considered. But if they deny the moral significance of the causal contribution of innocent threats and aggressors for the question of liability, they would most likely also deny the moral significance of the contributions made by innocent moral obstacles.

It is, however, possible to combine the idea of giving rise to cost with this idea of liability. One can hold that a person cannot make himself liable to defensive harm unless the person is morally responsible for danger to others but accept that there might be other reasons that could make it permissible to harm him other than the fact that he is liable. One reason could be that he gives rise to cost. In such cases, being a moral obstacle, physical obstructor, or passive threat would (somewhat) overcome the presumption against harming a nonliable person.

20. See, e.g., Jeff McMahan, "Self-Defense and the Problem of the Innocent Attacker," *Ethics* 104 (1994): 252–90, and "The Basis of Moral Liability to Defensive Killing," *Philosophical Issues* 15 (2005): 386–405; Michael Otsuka, "Killing the Innocent in Self-Defense," *Philosophy and Public Affairs* 23 (1994): 74–94; and David Rodin, *War and Self-Defense* (Oxford: Clarendon, 2002), 70–99.

The rationale behind the weakening of the constraint against harming moral obstacles is similar to the rationale behind the weakening of the constraint against harming threats and physical obstructors. The rationale is that it is important how our whereabouts affect other people, and it is not plausible that we should be allowed to affect them negatively (no matter how innocently and nonresponsibly) without being required to bear some cost (when cost must be borne). If we required the person under threat to bear the entire cost arising from the presence of the moral obstacle, obstructor, or threat, that would make an unreasonable demand on her.<sup>21</sup>

The theory of moral obstacles identifies a feature that moral obstacles share with obstructors, threats, and those who do or enable harm: that they typically give rise to cost. This feature has moral implications. Although having this feature may not make people liable to harm, I maintain that they are among the appropriate set of (innocent) people that could reasonably be required to bear some additional cost to help protect a person under threat. Relative to a situation in which a person is under threat of harm, all innocent people may be called on to bear some limited cost in order to help protect her on the basis of a duty of assistance. But there is a subclass of innocent people who may be required to bear some additional cost to further this purpose because they themselves give rise to cost. Moral obstacles are members of this subclass.

If we reject the idea that those who give rise to cost due to pure bad luck should bear additional cost, then we must maintain instead that those initially under threat must bear all the cost. Mary would then have to constrain her attempts to save herself and the others by taking care not to harm people—even if their presence gives rise to cost—as if all people she harmed were bystanders and not relevantly involved in the situation. That would limit her defensive options only at the cost of herself and those around her, and that would be unfair.

This fairness argument is unlikely to settle the controversy surrounding the moral significance of mere causal relevance to a harmful outcome. But it would be a mistake to dismiss the theory of moral obstacles on such grounds, especially if one accepts that other instances of mere causality have moral significance. Philosophers who have argued against the significance of mere causal relevance have typically done this on the grounds that causality alone cannot make a person liable to harm. And it may very well be true that a person cannot lose his rights against being harmed due to factors for which he is not morally responsible. But it is a mistake to hold that the constraint against harming a person can be reduced only if this person becomes liable to harm.

21. In discussing Thomson's example of the falling nonresponsible fat man and the problem of the innocent threat, Frances Kamm suggested that a "person's inappropriate location vis-à-vis another raises moral questions no matter how it comes about" (*Creation and Abortion* [New York: Oxford University Press, 1992], 47).

## IV. SOME CLARIFICATIONS AND OBJECTIONS

#### *Apparent and Beneficial Moral Obstacles*

The moral significance of being a moral obstacle is captured by the idea that obstacles give rise to cost by being in a particular place relative to a situation in which no one is in that place, all else being equal. When all else is not equal, the counterfactual may not hold. Suppose that if it were not for the presence of Mo, Mary would not be able to defend herself. Mo's presence is what makes her able to defend herself. Yet, Mary now needs to harm Mo in the process of defending herself. Mo could then be a *beneficial moral obstacle*.

Suppose, in a variation of MO, that the presence of Mo has led Tom to attack Mary in a way different from how he would have attacked her had Mo not been present.<sup>22</sup> The reason why Tom now attacks Mary in a different way may be because the presence of Mo motivates him to act differently or because Mo's presence makes him unable to use the means he otherwise would have used. There might be a morally relevant difference between these two instances, but I discuss only the latter type. Suppose Mo's presence makes Tom unable to use his napalm bomb. Had Tom used the napalm bomb, Mary would have had no way of defending herself. But due to Mo's presence, Mary is now able to defend herself against Tom's attack. However, she will thereby also harm Mo. How should we judge this case? I am not sure.

It is not clear that Mo's presence gives rise to cost. All else being equal, the absence of Mo would have left Mary unable to defend herself.<sup>23</sup> To justify harming Mo, Mary can therefore not say that his presence gives rise to cost. The presence of Mo is like the presence of a bystander; his presence provides Mary with an option to save herself that she would not have had in his absence (all else being equal). It is true that Mary has to decide whether to harm Mo or to let herself be harmed. But bystanders may also give rise to such choices. On reflection, I think Mary should treat Mo as a bystander when knowing the facts about the situation.

Sometimes it makes sense to differentiate the benefit-making feature of the beneficial moral obstacle from his cost-making feature. We could then say that the person's present situation gives rise to cost but that his past situation gave rise to a benefit. For instance, Mo's presence could have made Tom unable to put together his napalm bomb, and for that reason he now has to use some means against which Mary is able to defend herself. We could then say that Mo is a moral obstacle now but that his benefit-making feature of the past should reduce the cost he would be required to shoulder.

22. I owe this example to Kasper Lippert Rasmussen.

23. There will often be uncertainties about whether Mary would have had no option to defend herself if it were not for the beneficial aspect of the moral obstacle. This is likely to affect our intuitions.

The moral significance of being a moral obstacle has to do with whether his presence gives rise to cost. A moral obstacle's benefit-making feature should therefore reduce the cost he would be required to bear as a consequence of giving rise to cost. I will not try to settle the extent to which it should be reduced here, nor will I try to explore how it is influenced by an increase in time between the benefit-making feature and the cost-making feature.

Is Mo a moral obstacle when his presence generates a benefit? One way to explore this is to consider what would happen if Mo were removed or jumped out of the way. Would Tom still be unable to use his napalm bomb, or would his removal imply that Tom used the napalm bomb? If the latter, then Mary's current defensive means and Tom's not using his napalm bomb would depend on Mo's continuous presence. Mo would then not really be a moral obstacle according to my account, only an apparent one. If, by contrast, removing Mo would not imply that Tom become able to use his napalm bomb because Mo's presence permanently destroyed this option, then Mo would be a moral obstacle, but he would be a beneficial moral obstacle (beneficial in the past).

#### *Means*

Whether a person is a moral obstacle depends on the means the person under threat has available. For instance, in *FLAMETHROWER*, whether Mo is a moral obstacle depends on the means Mary has (and not only on where Mo is). If Mary had no flamethrower, Mo would not be a moral obstacle. And should the flamethrower cease to work, the people behind Tom would no longer be moral obstacles. This may seem counterintuitive. But observe that in such cases Mo's presence gives rise to no cost, and we could not plausibly claim that he should bear more cost than any other bystander.

It may also be worth observing that the doctrine of double effect would face a similar challenge, although it would be presented in a different way. Whether Mo can be harmed without Mary needing to target him or to use him as a means depends on the means Mary has. If Mary has no flamethrower, or it is not working, she is not able to harm Mo as a side effect.

But the type of means the person under threat has available poses a further challenge. In *FLAMETHROWER*, I indicated in footnote 7 that the flamethrower could be given a plausible context by assuming that it was used in war, that Tom was an unjust soldier, and that the people behind Tom were civilians. This is because if the means of defense are completely outlandish it may seem unreasonable to require a moral obstacle to bear additional cost as a consequence.<sup>24</sup> Let me explain.

A person becomes an innocent moral obstacle due to bad luck, and this has implications for the cost that can permissibly be imposed on him and the cost he would be required to bear to protect the person under threat. Yet, a person may become a moral obstacle not only due to ordinary bad luck but also due to *extraordinary* bad luck. When these extraordinary circumstances take the form of something that happens directly to the moral obstacle (suppose, e.g., some aliens have dropped Mo behind Tom), it nevertheless seems correct that he would have to bear additional cost as a consequence. It would be unreasonable to require the person under threat to bear all cost as a consequence of Mo's extraordinary bad luck.

By contrast, if what makes the situation extraordinary relates directly to the person under threat—perhaps because she carries some outlandish means of defense—then it may not be reasonable to require the moral obstacle to bear additional cost as a consequence. For instance, suppose Mary happens to carry a small atomic bomb that she could set off to defend herself against Tom (and extraordinarily enough, she is also carrying a protective suit that will enable her to survive the blast). All people within the perimeter of the explosion would now become moral obstacles to Mary's defense. But we might resist the idea that all those within the reach of the atomic explosion would incur additional cost due to their being within its reach. The means Mary has at hand seem too expansive for it to be reasonable to require those who end up as moral obstacles to bear additional cost.

We therefore need to delimit instances when what is extraordinary relates to the person under threat and not to the moral obstacle and when the defensive means of the person under threat would count as outlandish. In such cases it might be unreasonable to require the moral obstacles to bear additional cost. To specify this is a difficult task, and I will not try to do it here. But there need not be a clear demarcation line since a person's requirement to bear cost can be altered along a continuum.

#### *Scope and Limits of the Theory of Moral Obstacles*

Consider:

**ALICE'S RIFLE:** Like **FLAMETHROWER**, but there are twenty people standing on the roof of the house, all of whom would be killed by the flamethrower. Killing these twenty to save herself and the nineteen others would be disproportional, and Mary decides not to do so. One of the other nineteen—Alice—has a rifle, with which she can shoot any of the twenty behind Tom. The person shot would fall and make Tom’s attack ineffective. Since Tom is hiding behind some trees, Alice cannot shoot him with the rifle.

24. I am grateful to Lars Christie and Michael Selgelid for pressing me on this point.

In this case one could hold that the people on the roof are only moral obstacles vis-à-vis Mary. Since Alice does not have access to the flamethrower, they would not be moral obstacles vis-à-vis her. Hence, while it would be permissible for Mary to use a rifle (if she had one) according to this view, it would not be permissible for Alice.

To assess this claim, we need to consider the rationale behind the theory of moral obstacles. Recall that when a person A is under threat of harm and has a defensive action available to her, a person B is a moral obstacle if his presence has the consequence that B will be harmed, A will be harmed, or both A and B will be harmed in some measure. This is true about the relation between Mary and the twenty people standing behind Tom. But the presence of the twenty also has the consequence that Alice, Mary, and the other eighteen will be harmed, or (some of) the twenty people behind Tom will be harmed, or all parties will be harmed in some measure.

This indicates that my previous definition of moral obstacles would have to be amended such that it applies not only to the person A but to all those whose ability to avoid harm is affected by B’s presence when A abstains from using her otherwise harmless means. Here is a tentative expansion of the definition:

*Moral Obstacle Expanded:* When persons A and C are under threat of harm, and A (or both) has a defensive action available to her (independent of the presence of other people), a person B, who poses no threat or physical hindrance, is a moral obstacle relative to A and C if his presence has the consequence that either (i) B will be harmed (if A performs her available defensive action) or (ii) A and C will be harmed (if A completely restrains her defensive action), or (iii) all will be harmed in some measure (if A partially restrains their defensive action).

This implies—at least if Mary chooses not to use her defensive means due to the presence of the twenty in ALICE’S RIFLE—that these twenty people are moral obstacles relative to all of those who are under threat by Tom. Having assumed that it is permissible to kill one moral obstacle to save ten people under threat, it will also be permissible for Alice to proceed in order to save herself and the nineteen others.<sup>25</sup> There is another reason for thinking that the twenty behind Tom are moral obstacles relative to Alice. I have argued that a moral obstacle has a duty to bear additional cost to help protect people under threat. If Mary decides against using the flamethrower in order not to impermissibly harm these twenty, it seems quite plausible that they would have a duty to bear additional cost (relative to bystanders) not only to help protect Mary but also to help protect Alice and the eighteen others.

25. It would presumably also be permissible to kill one of the two on the roof if that saved only ten people, even if Mary were not among the ten. When discussing a related case, Kamm asks: “What if someone else has the capacity to permissibly do what would kill

#### *True Alternative*

A worry could be that there would be no fundamental distinction between being a moral obstacle to successful self-defense and being someone who must be killed as a side effect if self-defensive action is to be successful. It could therefore be suggested that I am not rejecting the significance of the distinction between killing as a side effect and killing as a means but instead offering an explanation of the significance of that distinction by reference to bystanders and moral obstacles. This would mean that the distinction between bystanders and obstacles would be a different pair of terms for describing the same phenomena that have traditionally been described using the distinction between means and side effects.<sup>26</sup>

Suppose that this were true. The theory of moral obstacles would still have significant advantages over the doctrine of double effect since it points to relevant features of the people who are about to be harmed in explaining why the constraint against harming them is reduced, rather than pointing to features of the agent that is doing the harming or the means that she employs.

But this is not correct. What seems true is only that in all ordinary cases in which a person is under threat and has a defensive option available to her that will unavoidably harm another person as a side effect, the person who will be harmed as a side effect is also a moral obstacle. This has led people to think that it is the type of agency that is important and not the circumstances of the victim.

But the doctrine of double effect and the theory of moral obstacles render different verdicts in situations in which it is permissible to harm a moral obstacle by using him as a means, even though there is no permissible option to harm the moral obstacle to that extent as a side effect. Consider:

---

the bystander but chooses not to do this. Does this give us license to do something harmful to the bystander?" To this Kamm answers in the negative ("Justifications for Killing," 660–61). I may agree with Kamm here, provided that the person is only protecting herself.

 ARMOR: Tom impermissibly attacks Mary with lethal means. She can save herself by killing Tom with a flamethrower. To the left of Tom is a person, Mo. If Mary uses her flamethrower she will kill Mo. Killing Mo to save only herself would be disproportionate, and Mary decides not to do so. However, Mo is wearing light armor, and can be used as a shield without being killed. But using Mo as a shield will impose some cost on him.<sup>27</sup>

26. I owe this objection to Jeff McMahan.

In this case Mary needs to use as a means a person that she is not permitted to kill with the flamethrower because doing so would be disproportionate. According to the theory of moral obstacles, it could be permissible intentionally to impose a certain cost on Mo when using him as a shield even though it would not be permissible to impose the same cost on a bystander, even if the bystander were also wearing light armor.<sup>28</sup> This seems correct. Mary may not kill Mo, but she may impose some additional cost on him because his presence gives rise to cost.

In contrast to agent-centered theories, a victim-centered approach like the theory of moral obstacles places no emphasis on harming and killing in a certain way or on the type of agency exercised. What is crucial according to the theory of moral obstacles is whether these people give rise to cost. In ARMOR, Mary may therefore permissibly impose a certain cost on Mo when using him as a means, even if imposing permissible cost on him as a side effect is not an available option, and it would not have been permissible to impose that cost on him had he been a bystander.<sup>29</sup> Being a moral obstacle is therefore not equivalent to being harmed as a side effect.

#### *Quinn's Distinctions*

In his discussion of the permissibility of killing people, Warren Quinn makes two distinctions that apply to actions of ending someone's life. The first distinction, between direct and indirect agency, is between the agent deliberately involving the victims in something in order to further his purpose (direct agency) on the one hand and the agent not involving the victim (indirect agency) on the other. The second distinction, between eliminative and opportunistic agency, is a distinction between two types of direct agency in which the agent intends to involve the victim. In opportunistic agency the harmed or killed person presents only an opportunity. In eliminative agency the harmed or killed person is an obstacle of some sort.<sup>30</sup>

27. I am grateful to Bashshar Haydar for presenting an early version of this case to me and for long discussions of the general idea of giving rise to cost.

28. I would think that Mary could impose just as much cost in this case as in Mo, but that is not essential to my position.

29. Since there is no initial permissible option that would not violate agent-centered constraints, we cannot appeal to Kamm's Principle of Secondary Permissibility to accommodate the intuition that it would be permissible to impose more cost on Mo in this case. See Kamm, *Intricate Ethics*.

One might suggest that the theory of moral obstacles is a variation of a distinction between direct opportunistic agency and indirect agency. The morally relevant difference between a moral obstacle and a bystander is that a moral obstacle, by his presence, creates a cost that he or the person under threat has to bear, whereas the bystander, by his presence, only creates an opportunity for the person under threat. One could therefore suggest that when the person under threat harms the moral obstacle, he is not taking advantage of his presence, not using him, and the agent is not involving the moral obstacle in his plans, whereas when he harms the bystander, he is taking advantage of or exploiting his presence—deriving a benefit that he would not have had in the bystander’s absence. One could therefore think that the feature I have identified is equivalent to the one identified by the distinction between indirect and opportunistic direct agency.<sup>31</sup>

But these distinctions are not equivalent. The case (ARMOR) that distinguishes the theory of moral obstacles from the doctrine of double effect would also distinguish the theory of moral obstacles from Quinn’s proposal. Mary’s agency is opportunistic in ARMOR, when she involves the moral obstacle in her project by using him as a shield. But it seems permissible for her to proceed. It is of course true that she is using him opportunistically only because she is unable to harm him indirectly without imposing disproportional harm on him. One could therefore claim that Mary is not really taking advantage of Mo’s presence and that Mary’s agency is not really opportunistic. If we try to save Quinn’s distinction by appealing to this fact, however, we would essentially have converted it into the theory of moral obstacles. We would not look at the agency that Mary would be involved in but rather look at whether Mo gave rise to cost.

One might nevertheless think that Quinn’s distinction has more explanatory power than my proposal since it appeals to the agency of the person under threat. But it is worth noting that Quinn’s distinction seems vulnerable to the same objections as the doctrine of double effect. Why exactly should the type of agency be important when we evaluate the permissibility of knowingly harming another person?

Recall the case Mo, and imagine that Mary can save herself by killing Tom at the cost of one of Mo’s limbs. Mary can, however, do this in two different ways. She can save herself and only in an indirect way make it the case that Mo loses a limb, or she can make direct opportunistic use of his limb. Assuming that both actions would have been performed with an equal degree of regret, my suggestion is that, in order to justify having cut off one of his legs, Mary would have to explain to Mo not the type of agency that she was engaged in when cutting of his limb but that his presence had the consequence that she had to let herself die or to take his limb. This would be the substance of her justification, not whether or not she acted in an opportunistic way.

30. See Quinn, “Actions, Intentions, and Consequences.”

31. I am grateful to Seth Lazar for pressing me on this point.

#### *Permissibility and Duties*

I do not take a stand here on whether there is a particular connection between a person's duty to bear cost and the permissibility to impose cost on him. My proposal is that it is permissible to impose additional cost on the moral obstacle because he gives rise to cost by being where he is, and the moral obstacle has a duty to bear additional cost because he gives rise to cost by being where he is (at least when he is aware of the situation). Neither of these arguments grounds the other. Both are based on the fact that a moral obstacle gives rise to cost and that it is fair that he bear some of that cost to protect the person under threat. Whether there is a difference between the cost the person under threat is permitted to impose on the moral obstacle and the cost the moral obstacle has a duty to take on to protect the person under threat, I also leave open.

It is, of course, possible to hold that it is permissible to harm a person to obtain a good insofar as this person has a duty to bear a similar cost to promote that good. Victor Tadros adopts this view in his book *The Ends of Harm*.<sup>32</sup> Tadros argues that it can be permissible to harm people when they have an enforceable duty to make a certain sacrifice in order to prevent or mitigate harm to someone else but are unable or unwilling to act on that duty.<sup>33</sup>

Perhaps it is true that whenever it is permissible to impose a certain cost on a person to promote a particular good, this person must have a duty to bear the same cost to promote that good.<sup>34</sup> But I do not need to assume this for the purpose of my argument. This is fortunate since I have already indicated that there might be a difference between the permissibility of killing someone and that person's duty to sacrifice his life. Moreover, to say that it is permissible to impose a certain cost on a person just because he has a duty to bear this cost does not solve the problem of justification. We need to know why the person has a duty to bear cost in the first place. This is what my theory explains for moral obstacles. A moral obstacle has a duty to bear additional cost because his presence gives rise to cost, and fairness dictates that he should bear some of it.

32. Victor Tadros, *The Ends of Harm* (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2011).

33. "It is permissible to harm a person as a means to an end if that person would have had an enforceable duty to avert the threat were she able to do so, even if, in exercising her duty she would be harmed to the same degree" (ibid., 129).

34. In fact, I have expressed this view myself in earlier work and written that "the permissibility of using force would be based on an agent's initial duty to bear cost" and that "just as we expect people to discharge their duties, they should be willing to accept that others impose costs on them commensurate with their duties when they themselves are unable to discharge these duties" (see Gerhard Øverland, "Forced Assistance," *Law and Philosophy* 28 [2008]: 203–32, and "602 and One Dead: On Contribution to Global Poverty and Liability to Defensive Force," *European Journal of Philosophy* 21 [2013]: 279–99).

### V. CONCLUDING REMARKS

The constraint against killing people in the process of defending yourself and others against an unjust attack appears to be weaker than the constraint against killing people in order to make the attack ineffective. Many have thought that this is because we do not intend the deaths of those who are killed in the process of defending ourselves or because we do not use them as a means. It is easy to understand why people have thought this; when we kill people as a side effect, we do not intend their death, nor do we use their death as a means for anything. This makes it seem that it is these features of the agent's actions that justify the weaker constraint against harming them. But this is a mistake.

The best explanation of the difference between the two types of killing, and the difference between two types of harming in general, is instead that those we need to harm are moral obstacles in one case and not in the other. A moral obstacle is causally related to a harmful outcome by being in certain circumstances. His presence has the consequence that the defending party, the moral obstacle, or both (in some measure) now have to be harmed. Being causally related in this way may give rise to cost. When a person gives rise to cost by his presence, some people have to be harmed as a consequence of his presence relative to a situation in which no person gives rise to cost in this way. It is therefore fair that the defending party should not be the only one required to bear cost. The person who gives rise to cost by his presence should also bear some of that cost. The morally significant distinction is therefore not one between killing people with or without intent or between using them as a means or not. The morally significant distinction is the difference between moral obstacles and bystanders.

# The Means Principle

Larry Alexander\*

### I. Introduction

Michael Moore believes there are deontological constraints on actors' pursuit of good consequences. He believes these constraints are best conceived of as agent-relative and intention-focused prohibitions such as "you must not intentionally kill, batter, rape, steal, etc."<sup>1</sup> I, joined in recent years by Kimberly Ferzan, believe that the best interpretation of deontological constraints—the interpretation that best accounts for our intuitions about certain stock cases—is that they are constraints on the causal means by which good consequences may be achieved.<sup>2</sup> We believe those constraints can be unified under a single deontological principle, what we call the "means principle." It forbids actors from achieving otherwise good consequences by using, without their consent, others' bodies, labor, talents, or other resources that are rightfully theirs. The means principle can be viewed as a jurisdictional limitation on the reach of strong (legitimately enforceable) moral obligations.<sup>3</sup> Its focus is on the causal structure of how good consequences are to be achieved, not on the mental states of those attempting to achieve them. Actors' mental states can affect their culpability but not whether their acts are morally permissible. Even with respect to culpability, actors' beliefs rather than their intentions are the primary determinants. Their intentions can affect only the level of their culpability if they are culpable, but cannot render an otherwise non-culpable act culpable. Thus, the means principle is a stark contrast to Moore's agent-relative, intention-focused account of deontological constraints.<sup>4</sup>

\* This chapter is a seriously abbreviated version, stripped of numerous citations of supporting literature as well as some supporting arguments, of the paper that can be found at <<http://ssrn.com/abstract=2378608>>. I presented the longer version of this chapter at a conference celebrating Michael Moore's seventieth birthday and then again at a conference on Deontological Principles and the Criminal Law hosted by the Rutgers Institute for Law and Philosophy. I owe thanks to the many people at those events who commented on the paper. In particular, I should like to thank David Brink, Kim Ferzan, Adil Haque, Heidi Hurd, Doug Husak, Michael Moore, Govind Persad, Re'em Segev, Victor Tadros, Peter Vallentyne, and Alec Walen.

<sup>1</sup> See, e.g., Moore, 2009d, 34–77; For Moore's conception of the morally and legally relevant notion of intention, see Moore, 2008a, 47–59.

<sup>2</sup> Larry Alexander and Kimberly Kessler Ferzan, *Crime and Culpability: A Theory of Criminal Law* (New York: Cambridge University Press, 2009), 96–100.

<sup>3</sup> See Larry Alexander, "The Jurisdiction of Justice: Two Conceptions of Political Morality," 41 *San Diego Law Review* 949 (2004). When I speak of strong moral obligations, I am referring to those the violation of which can be legitimately punished and thus result in a deprivation of certain rights. Weaker moral obligations are those the violation of which can be criticized and rightfully blamed. The means principle is a constraint on the former but not the latter.

<sup>4</sup> Moore views deontological constraints as agent-relative, moral-agent focused. See Moore, 2009d, ch. 3; Moore, 2012d, 459–61.

### II. The Consequentialist Background

Deontological constraints do not and cannot exhaust all of our enforceable moral duties. Many of our acts are assessable only through a consequentialist lens. In the famous *Trolley* hypothetical, turning the trolley to save the five trapped workers but killing the one worker trapped on the siding is generally believed to be a morally permissible act. (Nor should it matter whether one is *deflecting* the trolley or instead *initiating* a new force, such as lowering a drawbridge that will stop the trolley but crush a bystander; deflection is, after all, a form of initiating.) If such acts are permissible, however, it is because they produce good consequences, the saving of a net four lives.<sup>5</sup> By the same token, turning the trolley from the track on which the one is trapped to the track on which five are trapped is a morally impermissible act because of its consequences.

I am going to assume that a consequentialist moral theory provides the backdrop to my discussion of deontological constraints and governs acts that do not fall afoul of those constraints or fall within the prerogatives that are the flip sides of those constraints. I shall not elaborate on what that consequentialist moral theory—call it C—looks like. For example, it is a matter of indifference for my discussion here whether “The Good” in C is monolithic or pluralistic. The nature of C, important as it is, is not my topic here.

### III. The Means Principle

The means principle (MP) is the principal deontological constraint on the pursuit of C. In other words, an act that is required by C but forbidden by the MP is morally forbidden. The MP trumps C.

What is the MP? As I said in the introductory paragraph, the best interpretation of the MP is a causal one. An act required or permitted by C is nonetheless forbidden if the good consequences that are the bases of its endorsement by C are produced by the unconsented-to use of persons’ bodies, labor, or talents.<sup>6</sup> In other words, the MP enjoins the appropriation of another’s body, labor, or talents without that person’s consent where appropriation is the causal path by which otherwise good consequences are produced. Put somewhat differently, the MP is a jurisdictional notion: A person’s body, labor, and talents are beyond the jurisdiction of strong (enforceable) morality unless the person consents to subjecting his body, labor, and talents to its jurisdiction.<sup>7</sup>

<sup>5</sup> Note that I am assuming that the numbers (of persons saved) do count. On the question of whether and why the numbers count, given that each person suffers only his own harm, see John M. Taurek, “Should the Numbers Count?,” 6 *Philosophy & Public Affairs* 293 (1977). Taurek’s answer to his question was “no,” an answer for which I have some sympathy. After all, if five people die, it is not as if there is someone who will suffer the aggregate of five deaths. (One who *kills* five is, however, a worse killer than one who kills only one.) Most who have written in response to Taurek accept the non-aggregation of harms to different people but still seek an argument in support of the proposition that one should save the greater number in situations where not everyone can be saved.

<sup>6</sup> The MP also forbids unconsented-to use of resources that could not have been obtained except by the possessor’s use of his body, labor, or talents; or of resources conveyed to him by others who obtained them similarly. See text accompanying n. 10. However, for the most part I will drop the reference to such resources in elaborating the MP. One’s resources come within the MP only derivatively by virtue of the MP’s prohibition of unconsented-to uses of one’s body, labor, and talents.

The MP explains the intuitions behind *Trolley* and other stock hypotheticals. In *Trolley*, turning the trolley to the siding is not a “using” of the one trapped worker’s body, labor, or talents. One would turn the trolley to the siding even if the one worker were not there or could escape, because turning the trolley itself saves the five whether or not the siding is occupied. The presence of the one trapped worker only reduces the amount of C-benefit turning the trolley produces. And the same applies to *Drawbridge*, in which lowering the drawbridge saves the five by stopping the trolley but kills a bystander who otherwise would not have been harmed by the trolley.

On the other hand, in *Fat Man*, where pushing the fat man onto the track is the only way to prevent the trolley from killing the five workers, the fat man’s body is the means by which the five are saved. Thus, pushing the fat man *is* a violation of the MP. So, too, in *Transplant*, is carving up the one patient to harvest his organs and save five dying patients. In both *Fat Man* and *Transplant*, the causal path by which the saving of lives is brought about runs through the unconsented-to use of a person’s body. In *Trolley*, it does not.<sup>8</sup> In every case, the relevant question is: How does the act in question satisfy C? If the answer is that it satisfies C only by using someone's body, labor, or talents as a resource without the person's consent, then the act violates the constraint by virtue of the causal path between it and satisfying C.<sup>9</sup>

<sup>7</sup> See Alexander, “The Jurisdiction of Justice: Two Conceptions of Political Morality.” I should also point out that the MP is not violated by an unconsented-to use of another’s body if one is not touching his body and is merely somehow taking advantage of it while rightfully occupying certain space. Examples would be standing in the shade of another’s body or admiring another’s body.

On the other hand, things are less clear in the case where the *Strategic Bomber* targets the civilians but only because their location is his best evidence for the location of the munitions, his real quarry. Is targeting them a violation of the MP? I am inclined to say it is, but without strong conviction. See Victor Tadros, “Wrongful Intentions Without Closeness,” 43 *Philosophy & Public Affairs* 52 (2015), 63–5; Neil F. Delaney, “Two Cheers for ‘Closeness’: Terror, Targeting and Double Effect,” 137 *Philosophical Studies* 335 (2008).

<sup>8</sup> In certain of the trolley loop hypotheticals, where turning the trolley will not by itself save the five trapped workers (because the siding rejoins the main track short of the five), but there is a worker trapped on the siding whose body will stop the trolley, turning the trolley violates the MP unless there is a C-benefit to turning it other than the use of the trapped worker’s body. For example, if distance over the siding loop to the main track were longer than the distance down the main track to that junction, and turning the trolley would thus give the five workers more time to escape (or at least more time to live), turning the trolley would produce C-benefits other than use of the one worker’s body. That would also be true if there were a heavy object further down the siding that would stop the trolley were it not stopped by the one worker. See also Ingmar Persson, *From Morality to the End of Reason* (New York: Oxford, 2013), 146–7 (his example of *Double Saving*, which is analogous to the trolley loop hypothetical with a greater distance for the trolley to go if it is switched).

In other trolley loop hypotheticals, where the track past the switch is nothing but a loop, switching the trolley to the section of the loop on which one worker is trapped will save the five on the other section only by using the body of the one to stop the trolley, a violation of the MP. However, not switching the trolley will save the one only by using the bodies of the five to stop the trolley, which would also violate the MP, or so it might seem. See Alec Walen, “Transcending the Means Principle,” 33 *Law & Philosophy* 427 (2014). Yet, in the latter case, it is chance (the position of the switch) that will “use” the bodies of the five to save the one. It is as if lightning has killed five members of a shipwrecked crew, whose corpses can now be eaten to sustain the one remaining. Switching the trolley, however, would be like throwing a meatier crew member into the path of the lightning to kill him and save the leaner members, who otherwise would have been struck, killed, and eaten by the meatier one. Switching the trolley from the five to the one seems permissible only if there is some reason to do so other than using the one’s body (perhaps the loop towards the one would require the trolley to travel more distance before reaching the five, giving them more time to live or to escape). The same analysis applies to other trolley hypotheticals similar to the loop hypotheticals in structure. For example, in the *Lazy Susan* scenario, where the five trapped workers are on a segment of track that can be switched 180 degrees, and Fat Man is also on that segment but farther away from the oncoming trolley, there is a C-benefit, (more time to escape or live) other than the use of Fat Man for rotating the Lazy Susan segment and positioning Fat Man rather than the five trapped workers closer to the oncoming trolley. Thus, in my

I have thus far spoken of the MP as encompassing unconsented-to appropriation of another's body, labor, or talents. The talents part is perhaps redundant, as in the absence of the ability to read minds one can only appropriate another's talents through his labor. I include the reference to talents merely to make clear that appropriation without consent of another's intellectual or artistic creations violates the MP even if the creation is a song, a poem, or an idea for an invention or a story that has not yet been reduced to a tangible form.

In addition, the MP extends not only to the products of intellectual labor that do not employ any resources other than mental ones but also to the products of labor that employ one's rightful share of external resources, resources the rightful shares of which are determined by C. If one takes one's rightful share of external resources, then no one else has a claim on one's improvements of them. For were that not so, others would be appropriating not only one's rightful share under C, but the improvements produced by one's labor and talents.

Moreover, not only does the deontological constraint extend to the products of one's labor and talents that have used only one's rightful (under C) share of external resources, but it extends as well to products and resources that belonged to another but have been consensually transferred to one through gift, bequest, or exchange. (I leave open, however, whether one's C share of resources should be sensitive to one's other sources of well-being, namely the willingness of others to exchange with one or donate to one.)

One important point here, neglected by so-called "left libertarians," who endorse something like the MP but who advocate the equal distribution of natural resources, is that the MP potentially blocks such a distribution. The reason can be illustrated by a simple example I have used in an earlier article.<sup>10</sup> Suppose there are two people, Short and Tall, and one natural resource, apples on an apple tree. Some of those apples are on the low branches, within easy reach of Short. Tall, however, cannot bend low enough to pick them. Other apples are on the high branches, out of Short's reach but within Tall's. And some of the apples are on the intermediate branches, within the reach of both Short and Tall. The MP dictates that only the intermediate apples are subject to whatever C's distributive principle is, whether that is equality, priority, utility maximization, or

account, rotating the Lazy Susan does not use Fat Man as a means and is permissible. But see Persson, *From Morality to the End of Reason*, 146–7. On the other hand, in the standard trolley hypothetical, with five trapped on the main track and one trapped on the siding, it is not permissible to switch the trolley to the siding if there are six trapped workers behind the one on the siding and who will be saved only because the one is in front of them and his body will stop the trolley. For there is no C-benefit in such a case for switching the trolley other than to use the one as a means of saving the six. And Michael Moore's example of wearing a vest that gives one's dance partner an allergic rash, the treatment of which saves her doctor's practice—the C-benefit that outweighs the harm of her rash—is a using. See Michael S. Moore, "Responses and Appreciations," in this volume. The causal path by which C is promoted goes through an unconsented-to production of a bodily condition. something else. For if the low apples were to be distributed to Tall, or the high apples to Short, that could only happen if Short were compelled to pick the low apples and Tall were compelled to pick the high ones. That is, without Short's labor, Tall would be unable to obtain the low apples; and without Tall's labor, Short would be unable to obtain the high ones. The MP thus requires that a C distribution of natural resources does not distribute any to persons who could not obtain them except through others' labor.

<sup>9</sup> Alec Walen's notion of an unrestricted claim is almost identical to my jurisdictional version of the MP. See Walen, "Transcending the Means Principle."

<sup>10</sup> See Alexander, "The Jurisdiction of Justice: Two Conceptions of Political Morality."

There is a further extension of the MP worth mentioning. Suppose Al engages in conduct solely to make Barb suffer psychologically because Al derives enjoyment from Barb's psychological suffering. Were Barb not to exist, or exist but not suffer, Al would be less happy. Now Al might be violating C. But suppose his conduct is actually furthering C. Perhaps he gains more happiness from Barb's suffering than Barb loses. Perhaps Al is even among the worst off and Barb among the better off. Still, Al's furthering C through Barb's psychological suffering violates the MP. Al's using Barb's psychological suffering to further C is no different from his furthering C by using the fat man's body to save the five trapped workers.

Reflection on the preceding examples might lead one to the conclusion that the MP is really just equivalent to the following norm N: "Do not make yourself better off than had another person not existed by making the latter worse off than had you not existed."<sup>11</sup> And indeed, most cases of violation of the MP will be violations of N, and vice versa. Moreover, N would even appear to solve the so-called paradox of blackmail; for blackmail is conduct that violates N.<sup>12</sup>

There are two reasons for not equating the MP with N, however. First, N takes no account of whether the baselines for determining "worse off" and "better off" are justifiable. Suppose Barb, a candidate for high office, has cheated on Carl, her husband, and Al learns of this. Al can sell his information to a news outlet and make a lot of money. So suppose he does so. He is now better off than he would have been had Barb not existed, and Barb is now worse off than had Al not existed. Al has violated N, but he has done nothing wrong; for Barb does not deserve to be as well off as she would have been in Al's absence. She has been "used" but has not been wronged.<sup>13</sup>

Perhaps we could save N by adding a proviso that "better off" and "worse off" are to be gauged relative to a baseline of deserved well-being. There is another reason, however, not to reduce the MP to N. For the MP is violated, or so I would contend, even when the used person is, without his consent, made *better off* through the appropriation of his body, labor, talents, or psychological states. In other words, the MP is a constraint on paternalism (which might otherwise be required by C), whereas N is not. Even forcing another to labor or use his body, not only in furtherance of C, but for the benefit of the person himself, is a violation of the MP. So too is getting him to labor or use his talents by manipulating him psychologically through deception or through inducing unpleasant emotions, even if the deception and the unpleasant emotions will ultimately cause him to benefit and are consistent with C.<sup>14</sup>

<sup>11</sup> Walen appears to endorse N. See Alec Walen, "Wrongdoing Without Motives: Why Victor Tadros is Wrong About Wrongdoing and Motivation," 32 *Law & Philosophy* 217 (2013), 235–40.

<sup>12</sup> Other violations of N, similar to blackmail, are the so-called "spite fence" and other uses of property that the owner values only because his neighbors will pay him to stop.

<sup>13</sup> As I shall point out in the text at n.18, the MP can permissibly be cancelled and one thus permissibly "used" if one has acted culpably and is deserving of punishment.

One final point about the MP. It, like its close relative N, does not govern activities that we would and could carry on in the absence of those who might be harmed by those activities. For those activities, even if they harm others, do not use their bodies, labor, or talents without their consent. C, not the MP, governs those risky activities. Reckless behaviors are culpable and, if they harm others, impermissible.<sup>15</sup> But they are so generally by virtue of C, not the MP.

That is all I want to say about the MP itself. The core idea is that we are not resources for others' benefit without our consent. Nor are we resources for our own benefit except insofar as we ourselves determine. Enforceable morality has no jurisdiction over us as resources for its ends.

### IV. The Flipside of the MP: The Prerogative

The logical corollary of the MP is a prerogative not to be compelled to further C.<sup>16</sup> In other words, the MP entails a realm of moral freedom. (C itself may, and if C is indirect will, contain its own domain of prerogatives in addition to the realm carved out by the MP.)

To see this, consider *Trolley* again. As discussed, it is permissible to turn the trolley from the track with five trapped workers to the track with one. Such an act, which saves a net four lives, would further C, or so I shall assume. But even if turning the trolley furthers C, the person at the switch cannot be enforceably morally obligated to throw the switch. For to compel him thusly would be to use him as a resource without his consent and violate the MP, just as would compelling him to lie down in front of the trolley if there were no siding. Throwing the switch or not throwing it, lying down in front of the trolley or not doing so—these are all within the actor's prerogative. They are in a realm of moral freedom, not in the sense that they are beyond moral criticism, but in the sense that they are beyond rightful coercion.

On the other hand, if the trolley is heading toward the one rather than the five, switching it to the track with the five is not within the switcher's prerogative defined by the MP. The act violates C; and in prohibiting the act, the actor is not being used as a resource without his consent. Thus, his act violates C, and its prohibition does not violate the MP. His act can legitimately be forbidden on pain of punishment.

I said that the prerogative that is the flipside of the MP is an area of moral freedom but also that acts within the prerogative are morally assessable. What I mean is that the prerogative is the realm of the super- and suberogatory; the realm of virtue and vice. If one acts within one's moral prerogative, one cannot be deemed culpable—and thus justifiably punishable—for not furthering C, even if one could do so at little cost of time, effort, or expense. Not furthering C under such circumstances may well be suberogatory and thus morally discreditable. But it is not culpable and thus not deserving of sanction.<sup>17</sup>

<sup>14</sup> Is so-called “soft paternalism” a wrongful violation of the MP? If so, does that undermine the tenability of the MP? Or is it an exception to the MP? Paternalism is in general a difficult issue, and it is particularly difficult if one wishes to maintain that “hard paternalism” is wrong but “soft paternalism” is not. See Larry Alexander, “Scalar Properties, Binary Judgments,” 25 *Journal of Applied Philosophy* 85 (2008), 96–7.

<sup>15</sup> More on the distinction between impermissible acts and culpable acts in Section V, and on risking and the MP in Section VI.

<sup>16</sup> Just as the logical corollary of a prerogative is a deontological constraint (such as the MP) on others.

### V. Limitations on the MP

Is the MP absolute, or is it subject to limits, and if so, which? Consenting and promising are non-controversial limits on the MP. Indeed, I would argue that they are really internal to the MP, which refers to *unconsented-to* uses of one's body, labor, and talents—not limits on it. There are other possible limits on the MP that are worth discussing. One stems from acts that have imperiled others and that will result in a violation of C unless the one whose acts are the source of the peril uses his body, labor, or talents to avert the peril. For example, if a man has accidentally thrown the trolley switch and redirected the trolley from the track with one worker to the track with five, and still has time to throw the switch again and redirect the trolley back to the one worker, he has an affirmative duty to do so. His original act, however non-culpable it was, will violate C unless he throws the switch. And he can be legitimately coerced to do so without violating the MP.

Are there other affirmative duties to act, ones not based on one's promises to do so (as might be the case with lifeguards, nannies, spouses, police officers, etc.), or based on one's acts that have imperiled others? The duty of parents to care for their children comes to mind. Does that duty apply only to parents who have voluntarily assumed it, or does it apply to all parents, regardless of how voluntarily they became parents? That is a deep and difficult issue that I will sidestep here.

Another possible external limit on the MP is also controversial, but it is one on which I have previously taken a stand. I have argued that a culpable actor who has yet to be punished to the full extent he deserves may be used as a means to further C or to protect others' rights. The use of the culpable is itself limited by the amount of suffering he deserves for his culpable act(s) in excess of the amount he has already been punished.<sup>18</sup>

The final possible (and again controversial) external limit on the MP comes under the heading of "threshold deontology." If the actor need only lift his finger to save a drowning infant, or if the sacrifice of his life would save a million lives, does the MP nonetheless protect him from being coerced to do so? Most deontologists believe that the MP does not. They believe the consequences of honoring the MP should matter and limit the MP's scope. The MP restricts the scope of C, but C restricts the scope of the MP, or so it is argued. Again, I need not settle the issue here. My interest is in the nature of the MP, not its limits. I have written on threshold deontology, not to take a final stand on it, but to point out its theoretical difficulties.<sup>19</sup> But, whether or not it is a plausible limitation on the MP, it does not bear on the nature of the MP within the limits it imposes.<sup>20</sup>

<sup>17</sup> Note that the MP and its corollary prerogative *can* generate intransitive options. One can permissibly breach a promise in order to risk one's life to save a stranger, permissibly go to the movies rather than risk one's life to save a stranger (per the prerogative), but cannot permissibly breach a promise in order to go to the movies.

<sup>18</sup> See Larry Alexander, "Recipe for a Theory of Self-Defense: The Ingredients, and Some Cooking Suggestions," in Christian L. Coons and Michael Eric Weber (eds.), *The Ethics of Self-Defense* (forthcoming, 2015). There I also suggest that if an innocent bystander could justifiably be harmed as a side-effect of use of defensive force, perhaps he could also then be used as a shield—a means—for defense, if the amount of harm he would suffer as a shield were less than the amount he would suffer as a side-effect.

### VI. Permissibility versus Culpability

Moral permissibility turns on how things really are, not on what an actor believes. It is an ontic matter rather than an epistemic one. If there are five workers who will be saved by turning the trolley at the cost of the one worker on the siding, then unless there are qualitative factors that relevantly distinguish the one worker from the five, switching the trolley to the siding is morally permissible in fact, irrespective of the switcher's beliefs or motivations.

Culpability, on the other hand, *is* a matter of the actor's beliefs. If the actor who switches the trolley is unaware that he is saving the five trapped workers and aware that he is probably killing the one, his act of switching, though morally permissible, is highly culpable. Conversely, if the actor believes that by switching the trolley he will save the five trapped workers at the cost of the life of the one on the siding, then he acts non-culpably in switching the trolley, even if it turns out that the five workers were not trapped, or were not on the track, or were an optical illusion. For though his act was morally impermissible, his belief that he was saving the five and thus was acting permissibly renders him non-culpable.<sup>21</sup>

So far, nothing that I have said should be controversial. We recognize that one can be culpable for attempting to harm or for unjustifiably risking harm, even if the attempt turns out to be harmless or beneficial, or the "risk" of harm turns out to be zero. Indeed, we recognize as well that the culpable attempter or risker who is unknowingly performing a permissible act can be encouraged by third parties. By the same token, those whose mistaken beliefs lead them to perform morally impermissible acts—who in the self-defense literature are referred to as "innocent aggressors"—may be permissibly restrained but not punished for their non-culpable acts.

My next points *are* controversial, however. First, although the actor's beliefs affect his culpability, his intentions cannot render an otherwise permissible act impermissible. At most, the actor's intentions may aggravate his culpability if he *is* culpable. But his intentions cannot render him culpable. To see this, consider the actor who switches the trolley. If switching the trolley to save the five is morally permissible, and if the switcher believes switching will save the five, then his switching the trolley is non-culpable *even if his only reason for doing so is to kill the one on the siding*.<sup>22</sup> We want him to switch the trolley (it furthers C). And he has the prerogative not to switch it (by virtue of the MP). If the only motivation he has for switching the trolley is his desire to kill the one, then that motivation is C-useful. And if he will not switch if we will regard him as culpable for switching in order to kill the one, then it would be C-useful not to regard him as culpable.

<sup>19</sup> Larry Alexander, "Deontology at the Threshold," 37 *San Diego Law Review* 893 (2000).

<sup>20</sup> Suppose we can prevent the violation of the MP in *Fat Man* by merely snapping our fingers (an easy rescue) but doing so will result in the deaths of the five trapped workers. If ordinarily our prerogative against being used as a means is overridden in cases of such really easy rescues (the deontological threshold is surpassed), must we prevent the MP violation at the cost of the five? Is it different if *Fat Man* is just trapped on the tracks, and we can easily save him but cannot then save the five? Similarly, if we must choose between saving two people from a deadly natural threat or one person from a deadly MP violation, should we choose the latter?

For discussion of this issue, see Re'em Segev, "Should We Prevent Deontological Wrongdoing?" (forthcoming).

<sup>21</sup> Put differently, culpability is a function of the actor's beliefs regarding the magnitude of the risks of various harms that his act presents and the presence of any facts that could potentially justify imposing those risks, discounted by the probabilities of those facts. Culpability is thus solely belief-based, unlike permissibility, which is solely fact-based.

Now I realize that this is not an argument that will convince the skeptics. For not every belief that it would be useful to hold is true. In Kavka's Toxin Puzzle, the fact that it would be useful to believe that one will drink the toxin tomorrow does not mean that one can so believe. Beliefs aim at truth, not usefulness.<sup>23</sup>

So consider these analogs of the ill-motivated trolley switcher. We may need people to carry out various tawdry but morally permissible and even morally compelling tasks. We may need CIA assassins. We may need executioners for murderers. And so on. The MP prevents us from compelling people to perform these tasks. So suppose that the only volunteers we get for the jobs of assassin or executioner are people who will enjoy the jobs. Should we regard the executioner who enjoys executing convicted murderers, or the CIA operative who enjoys assassinating terrorists, as having acted *culpably* in executing or assassinating if their acts were morally permissible and they were aware of the facts that made the acts permissible?

I would contend that the answer should be "no." I believe that the temptation to say otherwise stems from confusing an assessment of character with an assessment of culpability. The executioner and assassin who enjoy their jobs may have character flaws that make them quite unsavory people. But that does not show their morally permissible acts of execution and assassination to be culpable. So long as they act on the intentions in question only when the acts are morally permissible—or would be morally permissible if what they believed to be true were true<sup>24</sup>—they should not be blamed or punished. And if they should not be blamed or punished, that must be because they have not acted culpably.<sup>25</sup> (Likewise, if a dosage of morphine is proper for a terminal patient even though it will hasten his death, then if the doctor who knows this nevertheless administers it only because he believes in euthanasia, he should not be deemed culpable for doing so even if euthanasia is otherwise impermissible. And if a bombing run has been pre-programmed by the Strategic Bomber and will permissibly bomb a munitions factory and in so doing also kill and terrorize some civilians, the Terrorist Bomber, who knows this, may non-culpably fly the plane as programmed when the Strategic Bomber falls ill, even though his only reason to make the run is to kill and terrorize the civilians.)

<sup>22</sup> See Judith J. Thomson, "Physician-Assisted Suicide: Two Moral Arguments," 109 *Ethics* 497 (1999), and many others in accord.

<sup>23</sup> Gregory Kavka, "The Toxin Puzzle," 43 *Analysis* 33 (1983).

<sup>24</sup> Applying this to what I have said regarding intentions, the one who switches the trolley with the intention of killing the one worker but believing that he is also saving the five workers on the main track is acting non-culpably *even if the five workers were not in fact trapped on the main track and were in no danger*.

<sup>25</sup> I thus disagree with Matthew Liao, who argues that because one can permissibly refrain from switching the trolley, one should do so if one's only reason for switching is to kill the one worker. S. Matthew Liao, "Intentions and Moral Permissibility: The Case of Acting Permissibly with Bad Intentions," 31 *Law & Philosophy* 703 (2012), 715–17. But the reason one is permitted not to turn the trolley is because, by virtue of the MP, one cannot be used as a means to save the five. If, however, one is willing to turn the trolley (in order to kill the one trapped worker), then it is good that one does so (as it will save the five), regardless of one's intent. Moreover, if we believe his act will save the five, we can urge him to switch, even if to get him to do so requires us to point out that the one worker on the siding is someone he hates.

If unsavory intentions cannot render a morally permissible act either impermissible or culpable,<sup>26</sup> good intentions cannot render a morally impermissible act permissible or non-culpable. The one who pushes the fat man onto the trolley track with the intention of saving the five, and who regrets having to kill the fat man, has still violated the MP and thereby acted impermissibly and culpably. A bad intention—say, the desire to kill the fat man and indifference to the fact that the death will save the five workers—will aggravate the culpability of the pusher. But the good intention will not eradicate his culpability any more than it will render his act permissible.

And now for a perhaps even more controversial point. Just as a bad intention will not render a morally permissible act impermissible or culpable (so long as the actor believes the circumstances render his act morally permissible), neither will it render a permissible act impermissible or culpable when it leads the actor to choose an act that is non-optimal according to C. So let us return again to *Trolley*. This time, however, in addition to the main track with five trapped workers and the siding with one trapped worker, there is a second siding with no one on it. Clearly, it would be C-optimal for the trolley to be switched to the unoccupied siding. But suppose our switcher, while aware of the five workers on the main track and of the fact that the second siding is unoccupied, is not motivated to switch the trolley to the unoccupied siding. He is motivated, however, by the prospect of killing the one worker on the first siding. So suppose he does switch the trolley to the first siding, killing the one worker. I would contend that he has acted permissibly and non-culpably, though surely non-optimally. He has revealed his character to be morally flawed, but in switching the trolley he has not acted in a way that merits punishment. Given that the MP permitted him to refrain from any switching, we should be grateful that his unsavory character led him at least to save the trapped five. Had he been unaware of them, then although his act would still have been morally permissible (because it would have saved a net four lives and furthered C), he would have been culpable for the switching. But because he was aware of the trapped five, his act was neither impermissible nor culpable. (Nor would the verdict change had he been motivated to kill the one in order to transplant the one's organs to save some dying friends—in other words, had he been trying to violate the MP. For, given that he was aware of the five, and the switching the trolley was not itself a violation of the MP vis-à-vis the one, it is immaterial why the switcher wanted to kill him.)<sup>27</sup> Some contend that using someone as a means itself relies on intention—the intention to cause another’s body, labor, or talents to produce a good result. This is not true, however. Consider this example. We have the runaway trolley, the five trapped workers, and Fat Man on the drawbridge over the trolley tracks. The drawbridge in its current position is crushing some lovely flowers, and Al decides to alter its position to save the flowers from being crushed. Al foresees—but does not intend—that altering the position of the drawbridge will cause Fat Man to tumble onto the tracks and get killed by the trolley. That would surely not be a justifiable cost for saving the flowers. However, Fat Man’s death will save the five workers, which would make saving the flowers overall justified were Fat Man not being used as a means. Nevertheless, he *would* be being so used, *despite the fact that Al does not intend his use but only foresees it*. (Al indeed regrets that the Fat Man would be used as a means because were the Fat Man absent, Al could justifiably save the flowers.) Using as a means does not require an intent to use. It only requires that the use is necessary to justify the act, and it is culpable if the actor foresees that the use is necessary to justify the act.

<sup>26</sup> I think we should be happy to conclude that unsavory intentions cannot render an otherwise morally permissible act impermissible. For that allows us to skirt the issue that bedevils those of the opposite persuasion, such as Moore and those who hold an intention-focused version of the Doctrine of Double Effect, namely how to distinguish what one intends from what one believes will result from what one intends. See, e.g., Moore, 2008a, 47–59. For an excellent critical analysis of the intention versus foresight literature and a proposed solution to its central problem, see Kimberly Kessler Ferzan, “Beyond Intention,” 29 *Cardozo Law Review* 1147 (2008).

Here’s another issue. May Al refuse to rescue Fat Man, who is on the trolley tracks, because if he is not rescued, the five workers will be saved? If one has no duty to rescue Fat Man, then refusing to rescue him for the stated reason is not wrong. Nor would one have a duty to prevent another from pushing Fat Man onto the tracks. On the other hand, rescuing him would not be wrong even though it sets back C (because four lives net are lost). For C is only set back by virtue of Fat Man’s not being a means to C’s promotion; and acts that set back C are not impermissible if they set back C only by saving someone from being an involuntary means of promoting C. And, *a fortiori*, if one has a *duty* to rescue Fat Man—for example, he’s one’s child, or one caused him to fall onto the tracks—then that duty is not canceled by the setback to C.

Finally, just as one’s intentions cannot render one’s act a violation of the MP if its causal structure is that it furthers C without an unconsented-to using of another’s body, labor, or talents, so too is the act–omission distinction immaterial to the MP. Both acts and omissions are encompassed by the prerogative that is the MP’s flipside. One who sees a rock thrown in his direction may duck it—an act—even if he is aware that it will

to the unoccupied siding. Given that at the completion of the first act, no one is in danger, would not the second act be an impermissible killing of the one worker because it is not a saving of any workers?

This line of resistance, which is limited to two-act scenarios, is quite powerful, and I am tempted to accept it as an exception to the claim in the text. Countering that temptation is this thought, however: If the actor will only switch the trolley away from the five if he can non-culpably switch two times and direct the trolley to the occupied siding, then should we not welcome his ability to do so? The point applies to all “package-deal” rescues that, because of the MP, one has no duty to undertake. If the package deal is that the actor will rescue the victim if and only if the actor may thereafter slug the victim, have sex with the victim, take the victim’s money, etc., may the actor permissibly and non-culpably rescue and then slug, etc.?

Here is another line of resistance: Suppose there is a deontological threshold such that the MP is overridden if the mere movement of the actor’s finger will save a life. And suppose this time that the first act of switching, which requires great strength, will direct the trolley toward the one worker. The second act of switching, which will direct the trolley toward the unoccupied siding, requires only the movement of the actor’s finger. Because of the MP, the actor is not required to switch the trolley to the occupied siding. Once he does, however, because the MP is now overridden, must not he now switch the trolley to the unoccupied siding?

Again, I find this line of resistance quite tempting when applied to scenarios that are structurally similar. Countering the temptation is the worry that an actor who will be culpable and thus punishable were he to stop after the first switching will just not switch at all, and the five workers will die. probably then strike and harm someone behind him, *and even if he himself would not be harmed by it were he not to duck*. Nor does one have to remain standing against Balanced Rock when one realizes that it has become unbalanced and will crush some picnickers below if one ceases to be its doorstop. “Ducking” by walking away is both an act and an omission (to remain in place) but is within the prerogative. For one has no duty to use his body to shield others even at little or no cost (unless his not doing so crosses the threshold of threshold deontology). Again his ducking may be criticizable as sub-erogatory, but it is not impermissible or culpable.<sup>28</sup>

### VII. When is Risking Violating the MP Culpable?

What risk of violating the MP are we permitted to take without being culpable? Assume, for example, that the agent is attempting to promote C (or attempting to act within his prerogative without reducing C). He estimates that his act is 80% likely to do so without violating the MP. But is that probability sufficient to avoid culpability? Consider, by analogy, whether an 80% probability of not punishing a criminal more than he deserves (including the risk of not punishing him if he is innocent) is sufficient to render us non-culpable in punishing him? Holly Smith argues that in assessing whether to acquire additional information in order to avoid breaking a promise, we should count the promise itself, as opposed to the harm to the promisee if the promise is broken, as having zero weight.<sup>29</sup> Assuming Smith is correct, should we treat the MP, as opposed to the harm to the one used, similarly? I cannot see how we could do that and still regard the MP as a deontological constraint on C. For if we assess only the underlying harm to the one used in deciding how to act in light of our estimate of the probabilities, we are engaged in precisely the decisionmaking that C, stripped of the MP constraint, requires. So we must give the deontological constraint of the MP a value apart from the harm of the using. Because we always run the risk of violating the MP—which includes punishing people more than they deserve when doing so furthers C—and of breaking promises, we need a theory for assigning such a value.

Here is the approach that I believe makes sense. First, the objective, God’s-eye view of deontological constraints looks like this: If the benefits of an act exceed its costs, it furthers C and is permissible. However, one counts as C-benefits only those that are not caused by usings (MP violations, including undeserved punishments) or caused by breaches of promises. On the other hand, one *does* count the harms to those used and harms to the promisees from breaches. Put differently, an act is objectively permissible if its benefits, excluding those causally derived from usings or breaches of promises, exceed all of its costs, including those caused by usings and breaches of promises. In *Trolley*, for example, one counts as a benefit the saving of the five workers, but one excludes as benefits the saving of lives produced by harvesting organs from the dead worker. The benefits of using him cannot be part of the calculus; only the harm of his death counts. Moving from the objective view to the subjective, culpability-determining estimates of the actor is now straightforward. The actor estimates the probability that his act will be permissible by estimating the probabilities and magnitudes of benefits not produced by usings or breaches of promises and the probabilities and magnitudes of all harms. If the net of permissible benefits over all harms, discounted by the actor's estimates of their probabilities, is positive, his act is not culpable (even if, from the God's-eye objective perspective, it will turn out to be impermissible). The key, I believe, to solving the problem raised by Smith is excluding all benefits derived from deontological violations but not excluding the harms.

<sup>28</sup> But if the picnickers had used their property as a brace to keep Balanced Rock in place, and someone removes it, thereby resulting in their deaths, his act is not within the prerogative but is a wrongful killing.

<sup>29</sup> Holly M. Smith, “The Subjective Moral Duty to Inform Oneself Before Acting,” 125 *Ethics* 11 (2014).

### VIII. Other Deontological Constraints?

Is the MP the only deontological constraint on the furthering of C? That is hard to say, because C itself has not been specified. I believe that most acts that we believe are impermissible and legitimately punished, at least if committed culpably, are either violations of C or violations of the MP. But I cannot rule out the possibility that there are some acts that are impermissible in this strong sense but that violate neither C nor the MP.
